- **A sight:** "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath" (Esther 5:9).
- **A demand, an expectation or a slight.** Rachel demanded children, and "Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God?'" (Genesis 30:2). Naaman: "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me" (2 Kings 5:11). Queen Vashti refused to come, and the king's "anger burned within him" (Esther 1:12).
- **A rival's honour:** the women sang of David's ten thousands, and "Saul was very angry" (1 Samuel 18:8). The elder brother heard the music for his returned brother, "was angry and refused to go in" (Luke 15:28).
- **A wrong done to another.** Jacob's sons were indignant "because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). David burned at the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5). Nehemiah: "I was very angry when I heard their outcry" (Nehemiah 5:6). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16).
- **Good done,** where it breaks a rule: the ruler of the synagogue was "indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath" (Luke 13:14).
- **A word that exposes.** At Nazareth, "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luke 4:28). At Stephen's speech, "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:57).
- **Something within.** "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1).

The verses show anger changing character with its circumstances.
- **Who is angry.** The same words are used for God and for people, and "for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9) is said in restraint.
- **Whether what sets it off is true.** Potiphar acted on a lie (Genesis 39:19).
- **For whom it burns.** For the widow and fatherless (Exodus 22:24); for the children (Mark 10:14); for one wronged (2 Samuel 12:5).
- **What it is joined with in the verse.** Jealousy (Deuteronomy 6:15); grief, "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5); the Spirit (1 Samuel 11:6); hatred, "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred" (Ezekiel 35:11); fear, "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged" (Daniel 11:30); compassion set against it (Hosea 11:8–9).
- **Time.** God's "for a moment" (Psalm 30:5) and "finished" (Revelation 15:1); a man's wrath kept "forever" (Amos 1:11); "do not let the sun go down on your anger" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Power.** The ruler's anger becomes a command (Daniel 2:12).
- **The one who carries it out,** and their own heart (Isaiah 10:7).
- **One and many** (Numbers 16:22; Joshua 7:1).
- **What meets it.** A soft answer, a servants' question, a father who comes out, a counsellor (Proverbs 15:1; 2 Kings 5:13; Luke 15:28; Acts 5:34–35). Or no one: "I looked, but there was no one to help" (Isaiah 63:5).

- **The measure:** "storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).

What decides is what the act is *for*.

Sin can be put away while a death still follows. Nathan says to David, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the Lord, the child who is born to you shall die" (2 Samuel 12:13–14).
A psalm says it of a whole generation: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psalm 78:50). Sin forgiven can still be followed by a death (2 Samuel 12:13–14; Chapter 2).

Sin can be put away while a death still follows. Nathan says to David, "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the Lord, the child who is born to you shall die" (2 Samuel 12:13–14).
A psalm says it of a whole generation: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psalm 78:50). Sin forgiven can still be followed by a death (2 Samuel 12:13–14; Chapter 2).

It shuts the mouth when the truth would hurt. "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15), and Eli had to press him: "Do not hide it from me" (3:17). David's servants "were afraid to tell him that the child was dead", and they said why: "He may do himself some harm" (2 Samuel 12:18). Here the silence is fear *for* the one who must hear. Elihu's silence was different. He held back before older men: "I was timid and afraid to declare my opinion to you" (Job 32:6).

And with God, the dead are carried, blessed and at rest:
- "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side" (Luke 16:22)
- "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13)
- David, of his dead child: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Samuel 12:23)
- Jesus, answering a question about the resurrection: "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38)
- "who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:10)
- The psalmist: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (Psalm 49:15)
- To the man dying beside him: "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43)
- Paul, weighing life and death: "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:23–24)
- "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In the same chapter he says, "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed" (5:4, in "Waited for", above). Both are stated
- Peter: "the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6)

Grief at a death takes more than one form:
- David fasted while his child lived, and rose when he died: "But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?" (2 Samuel 12:23).
- Later, "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead" (2 Samuel 13:39).
- Jeremiah turns the weeping elsewhere: "Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away" (Jeremiah 22:10).
- Mary, at Jesus' feet: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (John 11:32).

And the words that comfort fear can be used to deceive. Jael said to Sisera, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18), and then took the tent peg (4:21). Absalom told his servants to strike Amnon: "Do not fear; have I not commanded you?" (2 Samuel 13:28). The words are the same as God's "fear not" (Isaiah 41:10). What they are for is the opposite. Section 10.10 sets out the same words spoken in kindness.

**A plan meets another person's will.**
- It can allow for it. Abraham's servant looks ahead: *"Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me"* (Genesis 24:5). Abraham answers with what God will do, *"he will send his angel before you"*, and with a way out, *"if the woman is not willing … you will be free from this oath"* (24:7–8).
- It can turn when its own cost appears, and another can bind himself instead. The nearer redeemer first says of Naomi's land, *"I will redeem it"* (Ruth 4:4). Told that Ruth comes with it, he says, *"I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance"* (4:6). It is the same man in the same scene, and his will turns when his own inheritance is touched. Boaz had left room for that will and had bound his own: *"if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the Lord lives, I will redeem you"* (3:13). Ruth's choice frames it: *"you have not gone after young men"* (3:10). One will is bound to self-interest, one by an oath, and one, Ruth's, is given in kindness.
- It can press it until it gives way. Absalom invited the king, who *"would not go"*. Then *"Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him"* (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). The plan ended in Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab *"would not come"* twice, Absalom set his field on fire (14:29–30).
- It can bend to a crowd. Pilate had said, *"I find no guilt in him"* (John 18:38). Then, *"wishing to satisfy the crowd"*, he *"released for them Barabbas"* (Mark 15:15).
- It can try, and give way. Pilate asked, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up" (Matthew 27:17–18). He spoke again, "desiring to release Jesus" (Luke 23:20), and asked, "Why? What evil has he done?" (Matthew 27:23). "And their voices prevailed" (Luke 23:23). "he delivered Jesus over to their will" (23:25).
- It can bend to please. Felix, "desiring to do the Jews a favor, … left Paul in prison" (Acts 24:27), after hoping "that money would be given him by Paul" (24:26). Festus, "wishing to do the Jews a favor", asked Paul to be tried in Jerusalem, and Paul appealed to Caesar (25:9–11).
- It can stand against a plan. The centurion, *"wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:43).
- Others can hold it back or help it on. *"when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him"* (Acts 19:30). *"when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him"* (18:27).
- It can be held back by the owner of the field. "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them" (Matthew 13:28–29).

**It presses another's will.** Absalom invited the king to his sheepshearing. The king "would not go", but "Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him" (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). Then he ordered Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab "would not come", twice, Absalom had his field set on fire, and Joab came (14:29–31). Pilate had said of Jesus, "I find no guilt in him" (John 18:38). Yet, "wishing to satisfy the crowd," he "released for them Barabbas" (Mark 15:15). A will can be pushed until it gives way, and in these passages that is how the plan was carried out.

section: 2. Thresholds: the merry heart and the sad heart
paragraph:
- Amnon: "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine … then kill him" (2 Samuel 13:28).
- King Ahasuerus: "when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded … to bring Queen Vashti", and when she refused, "his anger burned within him" (Esther 1:10–12).
- The Philistines: "when their hearts were merry, they said, 'Call Samson'", and the house fell (Judges 16:25–30).
- Gibeah: "as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city … surrounded the house" (Judges 19:22).
- Boaz: "when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry", Ruth came to him and asked him to be her redeemer (Ruth 3:7–9).
- Nabal: "Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk". The next morning, "his heart died within him" (1 Samuel 25:36–37).
- Haman leaves Esther's banquet "joyful and glad of heart", sees Mordecai, and builds a gallows (Esther 5:9–14). Between the glad heart and the gallows comes anger: "he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (5:9), and "all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (5:13).

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

Grief at a death takes more than one form:
- David fasted while his child lived, and rose when he died: "But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?" (2 Samuel 12:23).
- Later, "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead" (2 Samuel 13:39).
- Jeremiah turns the weeping elsewhere: "Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away" (Jeremiah 22:10).
- Mary, at Jesus' feet: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (John 11:32).

It comes to everyone. "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48). The psalmist asks it inside a plea about God's anger: "How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is!" (89:46–47; 10.9). "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?" (Zechariah 1:5). Living forever was withheld at the very start, "lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever" (Genesis 3:22). And Job asks: "If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come" (Job 14:14).

Joab sent a wise woman of Tekoa to David with a staged plea: "Joab put the words in her mouth" (2 Samuel 14:3). In it she says: "We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). Death falls alike on those the world would set apart:
- "How the wise dies just like the fool!" (Ecclesiastes 2:16)
- "a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2)
- "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27)

paragraph: God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this.

A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).

**He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.**
- "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10).
- "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).
- In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).

"As the Lord lives" is its commonest form, and often a second life is joined to it, the life of the one spoken to. David to Jonathan: "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3). Elisha, three times, to Elijah: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2 Kings 2:2). Ittai to David: "wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21). I read the oath as placing a promise before the living God and binding the speaker to it by life.

Some hold to another even to death:
- Ruth to Naomi: "Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the Lord do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you" (Ruth 1:17).
- Ittai to David: "wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21).
- Peter: "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!" (Matthew 26:35).
- Paul, to friends who wept: "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 21:13).

Loyalty between people was sworn by life. Ittai to David: "As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21). Elisha to Elijah: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2 Kings 2:2). David's lament says it of Saul and Jonathan: "In life and in death they were not divided" (2 Samuel 1:23). Chapter 2 ("Living before God") gives the oath.

How a person rates himself, or another, can be put in the words "a dead dog". Mephibosheth to David: "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?" (2 Samuel 9:8). Abishai, of Shimei: "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king?" (2 Samuel 16:9).

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

The English word "fear" covers several Hebrew words, and they do not all mean the same thing.
- ***Yārēʾ*, "to fear".** This is the ordinary word. It is used for fear of an enemy and for fear of God, and turned round it describes the one who is feared: God is "awesome", the wilderness "terrifying" (Deuteronomy 10:17; 8:15).
- ***Paḥad*, "to dread".** This is the dread that falls on a person. Yet once the same word is used of joy: "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5).
- ***Ḥārad*, "to tremble".** This is the body's trembling. Yet Eli "was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13). That is trembling *for* something he loved, not *before* a threat.
- ***Rāgaz*, "to tremble, be stirred".** The earth quakes with it. A person is stirred with it to anger, "Be angry, and do not sin" (Psalm 4:4), and to grief: David "was deeply moved" and wept for Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33).

Wanting can read a sign before the news comes. As the runners came from the battle, "the king said, 'He is a good man and comes with good news'" (2 Samuel 18:27). His first question was not about the battle: "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" (18:29). The news was Absalom's death, and "the king was deeply moved" (18:33). I read the wish shaping how the runner was read.

The English "fear" covers many Hebrew and Greek words, and one word can be rendered many ways.
- ***Yārēʾ*, "to fear".** It is the ordinary word, used for fear of an enemy and for the fear of God. Turned round, it describes the one who is feared: God is "awesome" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and the wilderness is "great and terrifying" (Deuteronomy 1:19). It is also rendered as a way of acting: "One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil" (Proverbs 14:16).
- ***Paḥad*, "dread".** This is the dread that falls on a person. Once the same verb is used of joy: "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5).
- ***Ḥārad*, "to tremble".** The body trembles with it. Yet Eli "was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13).
- ***Rāgaz*, "to tremble, be stirred".** The earth quakes with it. The ESV also renders it "Be angry, and do not sin" (Psalm 4:4), "Do not quarrel on the way" (Genesis 45:24), and David "was deeply moved" and wept for Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33).
- ***Môrāʾ*, "fear, terror".** This is the word of "Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread" (Isaiah 8:13), and of God's "great deeds of terror" in Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:34).
- **The terror and horror words.** *Māgôr*, "terror", gives the name "Terror on Every Side" (Jeremiah 20:3). *Šammâ*, "horror, desolation", names a people as what others are horrified at: "I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" (Jeremiah 24:9).
- **The Greek words.** *Phobos*, "fear", and its verb carry most of the New Testament verses. The ESV renders the one word as terror, respect, reverence and awe: "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad"; "respect to whom respect is owed" (Romans 13:3, 7); "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21); "filled with awe" (Luke 5:26). With it go *tromos*, "trembling"; *deilia*, "cowardice"; *eulabeia*, "reverence"; and *ekthambeō*, "to be alarmed".

The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it.
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted.
- **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31).
- **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18).
- **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28).
- **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears".
- **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).
- **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Faith, trust and love** (the section above).
- **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side.
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

- **Thinking happens together.** The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest" (Mark 9:34). Shared reasoning can become a shared deed: "they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Let us kill him'" (Luke 20:14).
- **Reasoning together can become a quarrel.** The disciples' reasoning about greatness became "an argument … as to which of them was the greatest" (Luke 9:46). Paul tells the church to welcome the one who is weak in faith, "but not to quarrel over opinions" (Romans 14:1), and to "do all things without grumbling or disputing" (Philippians 2:14).
- **Thinking can make distinctions it should not.** When the rich man is given the good seat and the poor man told to stand: "have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:4).
- **The heart can be absent from the words.** "'Eat and drink!' he says to you, but his heart is not with you" (Proverbs 23:7).
- **Love does not keep the count.** Love "is not irritable or resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5). The Greek word behind "resentful" is the reckoning word: love does not reckon up wrong. It is the same word used of God, who in Christ was "not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Corinthians 5:19). Paul, deserted at his trial, prays: "May it not be charged against them!" (2 Timothy 4:16). The one who has done wrong asks for the same thing: "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong" (2 Samuel 19:19). David answered, "You shall not die", and gave him his oath (19:23). And where there is trust, the count is not even asked for: "they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money … for they dealt honestly" (2 Kings 12:15).

When David came back over the Jordan, three men met him. Ziba and his men "crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure" (2 Samuel 19:18). Shimei fell down before him: "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong … For your servant knows that I have sinned" (19:19–20). Mephibosheth had not cared for his feet or beard or clothes since the king left (19:24). Slandered by Ziba, he did not argue his cause: "my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you … What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?" (19:27–28). When the land was divided, he said, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home" (19:30). I read his loyalty in what he gives up: the king's return is what he holds to, not the land.

**Zeal put on show, and zeal that set aside an oath.** Jehu says, *"Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord"* (2 Kings 10:16). His zeal is something to be watched from his chariot. The same chapter ends on his heart: *"But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart"* (10:31; 13.1). Saul's zeal broke a sworn word: *"Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah"* (2 Samuel 21:2). The guilt outlived him. Years later there was a famine *"for three years, year after year"*, and the Lord said, *"There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death"* (21:1). I read a zeal for one's own people that set an oath before God aside, and a guilt that came due after the zealous man was dead. Phinehas's zeal was God's own, and the wrath turned back. Saul's was for the people, and it left bloodguilt behind.

The verses picture death as something that surrounds and holds. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me" (2 Samuel 22:5–6). It has gates: "O you who lift me up from the gates of death" (Psalm 9:13). God is named by the rescue: "Our God is a God of salvation, and to God, the Lord, belong deliverances from death" (Psalm 68:20). Even his discipline stops short of it: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death" (Psalm 118:18). Paul says it of a danger in his own life: "He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10).

*Held (working note, not part of the text):* the verses in which fear crosses into life and death are kept for Chapter 2, where that placement is on hold. These include the terrors at the end of the wicked (Job 18:14), terror "in the land of the living" (Ezekiel 32:23–32), terrors in age (Ecclesiastes 12:5), "the waves of death" (2 Samuel 22:5), and the deaths in Acts 5. Fear of death (Hebrews 2:15) and "the cowardly" (Revelation 21:8) are named above only as fear.

It is where people hold those they love. A mother lays her child "at her breast" (1 Kings 3:20). Naomi "took the child and laid him on her lap" (Ruth 4:16). "Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries a nursing child" (Numbers 11:12). "He will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom" (Isaiah 40:11).

A feeling can be about life itself. Job: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1). Under the curse, life itself is held in dread: "Night and day you shall be in dread and have no assurance of your life" (Deuteronomy 28:66). And joy can fill a life so that its days are not counted: "God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart" (Ecclesiastes 5:20). Chapter 2 ("Life weighed") gives the account. Feeling also reaches toward a life that is threatened. Before Solomon, the true mother is known by it: "because her heart yearned for her son" (1 Kings 3:26). And the man brought back from the pit "sees his face with a shout of joy" (Job 33:26).

A death can be felt as sin remembered. The widow at Zarephath says to Elijah, "What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!" (1 Kings 17:18). That is her reading, as the verse gives it. Elijah takes the question to God: "O Lord my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?" (17:20). The child is given back (Chapter 2).

- Elijah "asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life'" (1 Kings 19:4).
- Jonah: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).
- Job: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever" (Job 7:15–16). A few verses earlier he spoke of "the anguish of my spirit" and "the bitterness of my soul" (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: "When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions" (7:13–14). He says it to God, "Leave me alone" (7:16), and he does not act on it.
- Saul, wounded on Gilboa: "anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers" (2 Samuel 1:9).
- Job speaks of those "who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures" (Job 3:21), and asks, "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" (Job 3:11).
- Rachel, envying her sister: "Give me children, or I shall die!" (Genesis 30:1).
- The Preacher: "I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

What answers these wishes is seldom death.
- **Elijah** is given food, twice: "Arise and eat". He goes "in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights" (1 Kings 19:5–8).
- **Jonah's** wish came with his anger at God's mercy: "angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9). He is given a question about God's pity for Nineveh (Jonah 4:10–11).
- **Israel**, wishing they had died beside the meat pots of Egypt, is given bread from heaven (Exodus 16:3–4).
- When Israel loathed the manna and spoke against God, the answer was something to look at: "everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8).

section: 2. Thresholds: the merry heart and the sad heart
paragraph: Solomon's people "went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1 Kings 8:66). The Preacher commands the merry heart and gives God's approval as the reason: "Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do" (Ecclesiastes 9:7). And eating can carry the soul the other way across the threshold: the angel's bread carried Elijah from wanting to die to walking forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:5–8).

section: Breath lent, and held by God
paragraph:
God holds both ends. "I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Samuel 2:6). When a letter asked the king of Israel to heal a man of leprosy, he tore his clothes: "Am I God, to kill and to make alive …?" (2 Kings 5:7). And between the two ends, he keeps alive:
- "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine" (Psalm 33:19)
- "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right" (Job 36:6)
- Joseph to his brothers: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20)
- Moses joins it to the fear of God: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive" (Deuteronomy 6:24)

Scripture shows life coming back through each of the inner words.
- **The spirit returns.** Samson, dying of thirst after his victory, drank the water God gave, and "his spirit returned, and he revived" (Judges 15:19). Jairus's daughter: "her spirit returned, and she got up at once" (Luke 8:55). Jesus then tells them to give her something to eat.
- **The life returns.** Elijah prays over the widow's son, and "the life of the child came into him again, and he revived" (1 Kings 17:22). Elisha "restored the dead to life" (2 Kings 8:5). Even after Elisha's death, a dead man thrown into his grave, "as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived and stood on his feet" (2 Kings 13:21).
- **The breath enters.** Ezekiel is shown a valley of bones and asked, "Son of man, can these bones live?" He answers, "O Lord God, you know" (Ezekiel 37:3). God's word to the bones builds the body first, then gives the breath: "I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live" (37:6). Bones, sinews, flesh and skin come together, "but there was no breath in them" (37:8). When the prophet calls to the breath, "the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet" (37:10). In Revelation, "a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet" (Revelation 11:11).

Each person answers for his own. "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). "But each one shall die for his own sin" (2 Kings 14:6). Jesus says it of unbelief: "unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins" (John 8:24). John speaks of "sin that leads to death" and of sin that does not, and tells a believer to ask life for a brother whose sin does not lead to death (1 John 5:16–17). He does not say which sin leads to death, and I do not guess.

Some deaths are recorded with their inner cause named:
- "But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord put him to death" (Genesis 38:7)
- "the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error" (2 Samuel 6:7)
- "So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the Lord" (1 Chronicles 10:13)
- the men who brought back a bad report of the land "died by plague before the Lord" (Numbers 14:37)

A feeling can even kill the one who has it. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). Chapter 2 sets this beside the other ways that end in death.

**Jealousy in the body and between people.** Envy reaches the bones: "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Proverbs 14:30; Chapter 4).
