Of the dead: *"Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun"* (Ecclesiastes 9:6; Chapter 2).

section: What the verses say about it
paragraph:
Proverbs and the letters speak about human anger directly.
- **Its course in the fool:** "The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult" (Proverbs 12:16). "Surely vexation kills the fool" (Job 5:2).
- **Its company:** "Make no friendship with a man given to anger … lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare" (Proverbs 22:24–25).
- **Its fierceness, cursed.** Jacob over Simeon and Levi: "Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel!" (Genesis 49:7).
- **What can stand against it:** "Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?" (Proverbs 27:4).
- **Fretting:** "Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil" (Psalm 37:8).
- **Its judgment:** "everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment" (Matthew 5:22).

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

Scripture follows the wrongdoing through to death. "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). Death can be at work in a person who is still alive: "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). And some of what kills is named in the inner being itself: "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). Chapter 2 ("Death and sin") gives the account.

Scripture is honest that people sometimes want to die. In the words of Elijah, Jonah, Job and Saul below, the Hebrew word behind "my life" or "I" is *nephesh* ("soul, life"). Most other such wishes name no inner word at all.
- Elijah "asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life'" (1 Kings 19:4).
- Jonah: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).
- Job: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever" (Job 7:15–16). A few verses earlier he spoke of "the anguish of my spirit" and "the bitterness of my soul" (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: "When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions" (7:13–14). He says it to God, "Leave me alone" (7:16), and he does not act on it.
- Saul, wounded on Gilboa: "anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers" (2 Samuel 1:9).
- Job speaks of those "who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures" (Job 3:21), and asks, "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" (Job 3:11).
- Rachel, envying her sister: "Give me children, or I shall die!" (Genesis 30:1).
- The Preacher: "I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

*Working note, not part of the narrative text.* This section is built to take further reading on choosing. Expected additions, each to be woven where it belongs rather than added at the end:
- **Job's own voice about choosing** (Job 7:15; 9:14; 29:25) is to be set beside *Choices weighed by another*: the chooser's own words alongside the friends' verdicts. Job 7:15 is his own would-be choice of death, spoken to God in complaint (7:13–16), so it also goes with *Life and death set before a person*.
- **Choosing between death and life** goes with *Life and death set before a person*.
- **Will and resolve.** Planning and willing are now written (*Planning*, *Willing*), and the chapters they touch carry their parts: the heart (Chapter 4), the spirit (Chapter 6), feeling (10.1), wanting (10.6), plotting (10.10), fear (10.12), anger (10.13) and Chapter 11 §4.
- **Held, not in the text:** the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 ("the place that he shall choose") and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14 ("the place that the Lord your God will choose"). Whether it is more than a shared form of words is open. Deuteronomy 12 has now been read in full: the forms differ (*"out of all your tribes"*, 12:5; *"in one of your tribes"*, 12:14; *"within one of your towns"*, 23:16), and in 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. It stays held.

Scripture also speaks of the dead from this side of death, and there it says something different. The dead are silent and gone:
- "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
- "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
- "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
- "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
- Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)

Job sets a man beside a tree. "For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again" (Job 14:7). The man has no such hope in himself: "so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep" (14:12). Job does not stop at the fact. In the next breath he turns to God: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!" And he pictures what he cannot see: "You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). The despair and the asking stand together in one speech. I read "till the heavens are no more" as setting a limit on the not-waking. Job does not draw it out, and I leave it there.

God remembers too, and his remembering changes things.
- He remembers what we are: "he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:39). In that psalm this is his reason for holding back his anger.
- He is asked to remember mercy inside his anger: "in wrath remember mercy" (Habakkuk 3:2).
- He is asked not to remember sin: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (Psalm 79:8).
- He stops remembering when a person turns, either way. Of the wicked who turns: "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezekiel 18:22). Of the righteous who turns to injustice: "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
- Job asks to be hidden "until your wrath be past" and then "remember me!" (Job 14:13).
- He keeps a book of remembrance of those who feared him (Malachi 3:16).
- And he remembers in judgment: "God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath" (Revelation 16:19).

Job in his pain wishes he had been hidden from life itself, cursing the night that did not "hide trouble from my eyes" (Job 3:10). Later the same wish becomes a hope: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!" (Job 14:13; section 10.3).

Some of the time, the call is to shelter while the anger passes. "Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by" (Isaiah 26:20). That is exactly what Job had asked for: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past" (Job 14:13). God offers his people what Job asked.

It comes to everyone. "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48). The psalmist asks it inside a plea about God's anger: "How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is!" (89:46–47; 10.9). "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?" (Zechariah 1:5). Living forever was withheld at the very start, "lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever" (Genesis 3:22). And Job asks: "If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come" (Job 14:14).

- **Prayer lives in the heart.** It can be complete there without a voice (1 Samuel 1:13). "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lamentations 2:19). "With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O Lord!" (Psalm 119:145).
- **God speaks to the heart.** To comfort someone, in Hebrew, is to *speak to their heart*. Joseph "comforted them and spoke kindly to them" (Genesis 50:21), literally to their hearts. God says of his people, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her" (Hosea 2:14), again to her heart. "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:2).
- **Comforted as by a mother.** "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 66:13). Before it the people are pictured as infants: "that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance" (66:11), "carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees" (66:12). The act is being comforted. The delight is the infant's, in being fed, and the one who comforts is God (13.1).
- **God tests the heart.** "The Lord tests hearts" (Proverbs 17:3). And he forgives according to what he knows there: "render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39).
- **The soul is the self in address.** It is told to bless, to hope and to rest (Chapter 5).
- **Life is asked of him.** "Give me life" runs through Psalm 119, and each time it rests on something in God: "give me life according to your word!" (Psalm 119:25); "In your steadfast love give me life" (119:88). The life asked for is for keeping his word, praising him and calling on him: "Let my soul live and praise you" (119:175); "give us life, and we will call upon your name!" (Psalm 80:18). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **He holds the breath.** Daniel to a king who had praised idols: "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored" (Daniel 5:23).
- **Seeing and hearing him, and living.** "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Israel marvelled: "This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live" (Deuteronomy 5:24). Manoah feared the same: "We shall surely die, for we have seen God" (Judges 13:22). To Gideon God said, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die" (Judges 6:23).
- **Relied on in the face of death.** "we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Chapter 2 ("Facing death") gives the account.
- **Asked for a brother.** "If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life" (1 John 5:16).
- **Inquired of, not the dead.** "should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?" (Isaiah 8:19).
- **Told to depart.** Those who "spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol" (Job 21:13) "say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'" (21:14–15). The act is a sending away. It is argued as a sum: serving and praying are weighed for profit and found not worth it. Job answers, "The counsel of the wicked is far from me" (21:16).
- **Returned to.** Eliphaz counsels Job: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up" (Job 22:21–23). Then "the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver" (22:25), and "you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you" (22:26–27). The act is returning. Delight comes after it, and prayer after the delight. It is a friend's counsel, given as a condition.
- **The human spirit worships.** "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24). "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47). Paul serves God "with my spirit" (Romans 1:9). At death the spirit is what is committed into God's hands.
- **God's Spirit prays within.** "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). The Spirit "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit" (Romans 8:26–27). The cry to God rises from inside the heart, and it is God's own Spirit crying.
- **God knows the leaning before the deed.** "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- **God reveals in the night.** "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries … Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these" (Daniel 2:28).
- **God reckons, and faith reckons.** God counted Abraham's faith "to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). "Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Romans 4:8). Abraham, for his part, "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19).
- **His plans against are open to turning.** "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds" (Jeremiah 26:3). How his own plans work is in 13.1 (*Purposing*).
- **Plotting is turned against him.** "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hosea 7:15). The verse before shows the same people: "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (7:14). Nahum asks, "What do you plot against the Lord?" (Nahum 1:9), and names "one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (1:11). Plotting against people is in 10.10.
- **His word can be reckoned strange, and his name esteemed.** "Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hosea 8:12). Against that stand "those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name" (Malachi 3:16), whom "the Lord paid attention and heard".
- **Thinking done in his presence sees differently.** "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). What he had been thinking about was envy: "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3). In the sanctuary he sees it as "a dream when one awakes" (73:20; 10.6, *Jealousy and envy*).
- **God cannot be likened.** "To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?" (Isaiah 40:18). And God rebukes those who thought him "one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21).
- **The heart meditates on him.** "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **And he thinks of me.** "What is man that you regard him, or the son of man that you think of him?" (Psalm 144:3). "I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). And his thoughts are precious to the one he knows: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).
- **Sought, and not far.** Paul tells the Athenians that God set the times and places of the nations *"that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us"* (Acts 17:27). The seeking is a groping in the dark; the one sought is close by. The next verse is *"In him we live and move and have our being"* (17:28; Chapter 2).
- **Recognised, and gone to.** At the lake, *"That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!' When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land"* (John 21:7–8). One sees and says it; one hears and leaps; the others come in with the catch. I read the same recognition met in three ways, none of them rebuked.

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

Deliverance from death is **for** something: for walking before God among the living, and for telling of him. "I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the Lord" (Psalm 118:17). And sometimes it comes by a price. Elihu tells of a man brought near death by pain, "so that his life loathes bread", until "His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death" (Job 33:20, 22). A messenger says, "Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom" (33:24). Then "man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy" (33:26). The man owns his wrong and his rescue together: "I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light" (33:27–28). Elihu ends, "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life" (33:29–30). No human can do this: "Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48).

Even an ordinary waking is credited to God. David fled from Absalom while "many are saying of my soul, 'There is no salvation for him in God.'" He writes, "I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the Lord sustained me. I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around" (Psalm 3:2, 5–6). The waking releases the fear. Another psalm wakes to God's presence: "I awake, and I am still with you" (Psalm 139:18).

Scripture also speaks of the dead from this side of death, and there it says something different. The dead are silent and gone:
- "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
- "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
- "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
- "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
- Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)

The verses picture death as something that surrounds and holds. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me" (2 Samuel 22:5–6). It has gates: "O you who lift me up from the gates of death" (Psalm 9:13). God is named by the rescue: "Our God is a God of salvation, and to God, the Lord, belong deliverances from death" (Psalm 68:20). Even his discipline stops short of it: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death" (Psalm 118:18). Paul says it of a danger in his own life: "He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10).

Scripture does not make the coming of death a calm thing. It shows the inner being under it:
- "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me" (Psalm 55:4)
- David to Jonathan: "there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3)
- "Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death" (Psalm 13:3)
- In Gethsemane: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38)

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

paragraph:
Many verses speak of the soul being "delivered from" Sheol or death. Sheol is the grave, the realm of the dead. Read in place, most of them are about a **living person rescued from dying**. Of the fifteen verses that speak of a soul delivered from death, Sheol or the pit, twelve are about someone kept from dying or brought back from near it. Two look beyond death (Psalm 49:15 and 16:10, taken up above in "Soul, spirit and heart at death"), and one says that no one can do it (Psalm 89:48, below).
- "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me … Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" The psalmist then turns to his own soul: "Return, O my soul, to your rest". And he declares: "For you have delivered my soul from death" (Psalm 116:3–8).
- "You have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psalm 56:13).
- "O Lord, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit" (Psalm 30:3).
- "You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again" (Psalm 71:20).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph: And one thing I did not expect: **the heart can die before the body does**. When Nabal sobered up and heard how close he had come to disaster, "his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (1 Samuel 25:37–38). The heart died first; the man died ten days later. The psalmist knows a similar death in life: "I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel" (Psalm 31:12). Literally, forgotten *from the heart*.

section: Breath lent, and held by God
paragraph:
God holds both ends. "I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Samuel 2:6). When a letter asked the king of Israel to heal a man of leprosy, he tore his clothes: "Am I God, to kill and to make alive …?" (2 Kings 5:7). And between the two ends, he keeps alive:
- "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine" (Psalm 33:19)
- "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right" (Job 36:6)
- Joseph to his brothers: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20)
- Moses joins it to the fear of God: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive" (Deuteronomy 6:24)

When life is in danger, the picture is turned toward God. Each of these calls on God to wake comes where the psalmist's life is at stake:
- "let him trample my life to the ground … awake for me" (Psalm 7:5–6)
- "Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! … Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication" (Psalm 35:17, 23)
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long … Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself!" (Psalm 44:22–23)
- "For behold, they lie in wait for my life … Awake, come to meet me, and see!" (Psalm 59:3–4)
- "stir up your might and come to save us!" (Psalm 80:2), in a psalm that asks, "give us life" (80:18)

When life is in danger, people call on God to wake: "Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!" (Psalm 44:23). Scripture also says, "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4), and I leave the two side by side. Chapter 2 ("Sleep and waking") gives the account.

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). And with God, the dead are carried, blessed and at rest:

- "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13)

- Jesus, answering a question about the resurrection: "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38)
- "who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:10)
- The psalmist: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (Psalm 49:15)
- To the man dying beside him: "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43)

- "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In the same chapter he says, "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed" (5:4, in "Waited for", above). Both are stated
- Peter: "the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6)

paragraph: The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

Scripture does not make the coming of death a calm thing. It shows the inner being under it:
- "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me" (Psalm 55:4)
- David to Jonathan: "there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3)
- "Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death" (Psalm 13:3)
- In Gethsemane: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38)

Much of what Scripture says about anger is about anger between people.
- **Kinship stops strife, or feeds it.** Abram: "Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kinsmen" (Genesis 13:8). He gave Lot the choice. In another quarrel, kinship is the weapon: "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter?" (2 Samuel 19:42). And "a brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city" (Proverbs 18:19).
- **Anger at a brother is judged like murder, and worship waits on peace.** "Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment … First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift" (Matthew 5:22, 24).
- **The anger of the powerful decides others' fate.** "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion" (Proverbs 19:12). Those under it plead (Genesis 44:18), read it as a sign ("if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him", 1 Samuel 20:7), or reach it through a go-between (Acts 12:20). Its favour has a ground too: *"A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully"* (Proverbs 14:35); *"his favor is like dew on the grass"* (19:12).
- **The law allows for heat.** The cities of refuge exist *"lest the avenger of blood in hot anger pursue the manslayer and overtake him, because the way is long, and strike him fatally, though the man did not deserve to die, since he had not hated his neighbor in the past"* (Deuteronomy 19:6). The Hebrew is literally "while his heart is hot". The law does not deny the grief. It puts a distance between the heat and the act, because the heat will not tell the innocent from the guilty.
- **The oppressor's wrath is shown with its end in view.** The king of Babylon "ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution" (Isaiah 14:6). The taunt over him begins "How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!" (14:4), and ends "The whole earth is at rest and quiet" (14:7).
- **A leader's anger can yield to a reason.** Moses was angry at Aaron's sons. When Aaron explained, "when Moses heard that, he approved" (Leviticus 10:20).
- **Anger is learned.** "Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare" (Proverbs 22:24–25).
- **Strife has a source inside.** "Your passions are at war within you" (James 4:1). Chapter 10.6 follows that.
- **It wears a household down.** "It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife" (Proverbs 21:9). The image is "a continual dripping on a rainy day" (27:15): duration, not a storm.
- **The one attacked feels it inside.** "In anger they bear a grudge against me. My heart is in anguish within me" (Psalm 55:3–4).
- **The trembling word is used of quarrel and rage.** Joseph sends his brothers home with "Do not quarrel on the way" (Genesis 45:24), and the word is *rāgaz*, "to tremble". "If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet" (Proverbs 29:9).
- **Love does not get provoked.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **One person's sin can bring trouble on many.** David, under the plague, asks to bear it alone: "these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house" (2 Samuel 24:17).
- **Vengeance is left to God.** "Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God … if your enemy is hungry, feed him" (Romans 12:19–20).

section: Fear that comes upon a person
paragraph:
Fear is felt in the heart and the body together.
- "he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly" (1 Samuel 28:5)
- "My flesh trembles for fear of you" (Psalm 119:120)
- "My heart is in anguish within me … Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me" (Psalm 55:4–5)
- "fighting without and fear within" (2 Corinthians 7:5)

- "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me … Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" - "You have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psalm 56:13).
- "O Lord, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit" (Psalm 30:3).
- "You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again" (Psalm 71:20).

The verses picture death as something that surrounds and holds. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me" (2 Samuel 22:5–6). It has gates: "O you who lift me up from the gates of death" (Psalm 9:13). God is named by the rescue: "Our God is a God of salvation, and to God, the Lord, belong deliverances from death" (Psalm 68:20). Even his discipline stops short of it: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death" (Psalm 118:18). Paul says it of a danger in his own life: "He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10).

God swears by his own life in judgment as well as in mercy. "As I live, declares the Lord God, I will not be inquired of by you" (Ezekiel 20:3). To Edom: "therefore, as I live, declares the Lord God, I will deal with you according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them" (Ezekiel 35:11). His anger can reach life itself: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death, but gave their lives over to the plague" (Psalm 78:50). Of Korah's company: "and they go down alive into Sheol, then you shall know that these men have despised the Lord" (Numbers 16:30). Chapter 2 (*Living before God*) gives the oath.
A psalm says it of a whole generation: "He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death" (Psalm 78:50). Sin forgiven can still be followed by a death (2 Samuel 12:13–14; Chapter 2).

paragraph: Life can be worn down. "For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing" (Psalm 31:10). "For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol" (Psalm 88:3). Under the curse, "Your life shall hang in doubt before you. Night and day you shall be in dread and have no assurance of your life" (Deuteronomy 28:66). Paul says of Asia, "we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself" (2 Corinthians 1:8).

Being reckoned is felt from the inside.
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22).
- "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3).
- A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9).
- Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13).
- A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).

The living can also feel themselves among the dead. "like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more" (Psalm 88:5). "For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground; he has made me sit in darkness like those long dead" (Psalm 143:3). "among those in full vigor we are like dead men" (Isaiah 59:10). It is on "those dwelling in the region and shadow of death" that "a light has dawned" (Matthew 4:16).

It comes to everyone. "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48). The psalmist asks it inside a plea about God's anger: "How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is!" (89:46–47; 10.9). "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?" (Zechariah 1:5). Living forever was withheld at the very start, "lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever" (Genesis 3:22). And Job asks: "If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come" (Job 14:14).

paragraph: Deliverance from death is **for** something: for walking before God among the living, and for telling of him. "I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the Lord" (Psalm 118:17). And sometimes it comes by a price. Elihu tells of a man brought near death by pain, "so that his life loathes bread", until "His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death" (Job 33:20, 22). A messenger says, "Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom" (33:24). Then "man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy" (33:26). The man owns his wrong and his rescue together: "I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light" (33:27–28). Elihu ends, "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life" (33:29–30). No human can do this: "Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48).

paragraph:
Two words name losing heart: the Hebrew *kāʾāh*, "to be disheartened", and the Greek *athumeō*, "to lose heart", literally to be without *thumos*, "passion, spirit". Between them they are used five times, and in every one someone or something else does it to the person.
- **A father.** "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21).
- **False prophets.** "You have disheartened the righteous falsely, although I have not grieved him" (Ezekiel 13:22). God says plainly that the grief did not come from him. It came from a lie.
- **The oppressor.** "The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might" (Psalm 10:10). The one who presses them down, in the next verse, "says in his heart, 'God has forgotten'" (10:11).
- **The persecutor.** He "pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death" (Psalm 109:16).
- **A defeat.** Of a king turned back by the ships of Kittim: "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Daniel 11:30). Here losing heart turns into rage. Two verses earlier, "his heart shall be set against the holy covenant" (11:28). His rage goes against what his heart was already set against.

section: From the heart to the mouth
paragraph: Cursing can become what a person wears. "For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death. He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him! He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones!" (Psalm 109:16–18). The act is cursing. Loving it, and taking no delight in blessing, measure how wholly he gave himself to it. I read the figure as speech that goes back into the speaker: put on as a coat, then soaked into the bones.

Scripture also speaks of the dead from this side of death, and there it says something different. The dead are silent and gone:
- "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
- "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
- "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
- "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
- Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)
