- "You have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psalm 56:13).
- "O Lord, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit" (Psalm 30:3).
- "You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again" (Psalm 71:20).

The death of his own is not taken lightly either: *"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints"* (Psalm 116:15). The word is not delight but "precious": weighty, costly. The psalmist had been in *"the snares of death"* (116:3) and was delivered (116:8). I read: not glad of it, but not careless of it. The same word was used between two men: *"my life was precious in your eyes this day"* (1 Samuel 26:21; Chapter 5).

Many verses speak of the soul being "delivered from" Sheol or death. Sheol is the grave, the realm of the dead. Read in place, most of them are about a **living person rescued from dying**. Of the fifteen verses that speak of a soul delivered from death, Sheol or the pit, twelve are about someone kept from dying or brought back from near it. Two look beyond death (Psalm 49:15 and 16:10, taken up above in "Soul, spirit and heart at death"), and one says that no one can do it (Psalm 89:48, below).
- "The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me … Then I called on the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, I pray, deliver my soul!'" The psalmist then turns to his own soul: "Return, O my soul, to your rest". And he declares: "For you have delivered my soul from death" (Psalm 116:3–8).
- "You have delivered my soul from death … that I may walk before God in the light of life" (Psalm 56:13).
- "O Lord, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit" (Psalm 30:3).
- "You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again" (Psalm 71:20).

section: The soul is hunted and rescued
paragraph: Because the soul is the life, it is the thing at stake. Enemies "seek my life". The false prophetesses hunt souls like birds (Ezekiel 13:18–20). And the soul is what God delivers: "You have delivered my soul from death" (Psalm 116:8). "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). Words reach it too: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25).

The death of his own is not taken lightly either: *"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints"* (Psalm 116:15). The word is not delight but "precious": weighty, costly. The psalmist had been in *"the snares of death"* (116:3) and was delivered (116:8). I read: not glad of it, but not careless of it. The same word was used between two men: *"my life was precious in your eyes this day"* (1 Samuel 26:21; Chapter 5).

The death of those who belong to God is seen by him. "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Psalm 116:15). Balaam says, "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). "The righteous finds refuge in his death" (Proverbs 14:32). Hebrews says of the patriarchs, "These all died in faith, not having received the things promised" (Hebrews 11:13), and of Abel, "through his faith, though he died, he still speaks" (Hebrews 11:4). Jesus speaks of a death that bears fruit: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24).

The death of his own is not taken lightly either: *"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints"* (Psalm 116:15). The word is not delight but "precious": weighty, costly. The psalmist had been in *"the snares of death"* (116:3) and was delivered (116:8). I read: not glad of it, but not careless of it. The same word was used between two men: *"my life was precious in your eyes this day"* (1 Samuel 26:21; Chapter 5).

Deliverance from death is **for** something: for walking before God among the living, and for telling of him. "I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the Lord" (Psalm 118:17). And sometimes it comes by a price. Elihu tells of a man brought near death by pain, "so that his life loathes bread", until "His soul draws near the pit, and his life to those who bring death" (Job 33:20, 22). A messenger says, "Deliver him from going down into the pit; I have found a ransom" (33:24). Then "man prays to God, and he accepts him; he sees his face with a shout of joy" (33:26). The man owns his wrong and his rescue together: "I sinned and perverted what was right, and it was not repaid to me. He has redeemed my soul from going down into the pit, and my life shall look upon the light" (33:27–28). Elihu ends, "Behold, God does all these things, twice, three times, with a man, to bring back his soul from the pit, that he may be lighted with the light of life" (33:29–30). No human can do this: "Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48).

The verses picture death as something that surrounds and holds. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me" (2 Samuel 22:5–6). It has gates: "O you who lift me up from the gates of death" (Psalm 9:13). God is named by the rescue: "Our God is a God of salvation, and to God, the Lord, belong deliverances from death" (Psalm 68:20). Even his discipline stops short of it: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death" (Psalm 118:18). Paul says it of a danger in his own life: "He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us" (2 Corinthians 1:10).

I read these as speaking from how it feels when God does not act. Scripture also says, "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4). Both are stated. I leave them side by side. Paul quotes the cry of Psalm 44 and answers it: "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Romans 8:36–37).

When life is in danger, people call on God to wake: "Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!" (Psalm 44:23). Scripture also says, "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4), and I leave the two side by side. Chapter 2 ("Sleep and waking") gives the account.

The living can also feel themselves among the dead. "like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more" (Psalm 88:5). "For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground; he has made me sit in darkness like those long dead" (Psalm 143:3). "among those in full vigor we are like dead men" (Isaiah 59:10). It is on "those dwelling in the region and shadow of death" that "a light has dawned" (Matthew 4:16).

section: 3. The parts give way in sequence
paragraph: Psalm 143 shows a collapse spreading from one part to the next, then turning. "The enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground" (143:3). "Therefore my spirit faints within me; my heart within me is appalled" (143:4). Then a turn: "I remember the days of old" (143:5), and "my soul thirsts for you like a parched land" (143:6).

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)

Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
- "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
- "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
- Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21)

section: Loving and hating one's own soul
paragraph: One more thread surprised me. In Proverbs, loving your own soul is wisdom: "Whoever gets sense loves his own soul" (Proverbs 19:8). "He who fails to find me injures himself" (Proverbs 8:36). In the Gospels the same words seem to reverse: "Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life" (John 12:25). The other Gospels put it as wanting: "whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25; Mark 8:35; Luke 9:24). Paul lives it: "I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course" (Acts 20:24).

"Behold, all souls are mine … the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). In the law, "if anyone [a soul] sins" is the ordinary way to begin a case (Leviticus 5:1). The soul here is the person who is accountable. The one who did the wrong carries the guilt, and it is their life that is at stake. The soul can also be harmed by its own wrongdoing: "he who fails to find me injures himself" (Proverbs 8:36).

**Whom he is pleased with.** At Jesus' baptism *"the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased'"* (Luke 3:22). In one verse the voice from heaven speaks, the Son is named, and the Spirit comes down. Matthew applies Isaiah's *"my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased"* to Jesus (Matthew 12:18; *Choosing*). Paul says that God *"was pleased to reveal his Son to me"* (Galatians 1:16). And of one who turns back: *"my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him"* (Hebrews 10:38). Wisdom says that favour is found by finding her: *"For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death"* (Proverbs 8:35–36). The finding is by daily waiting, *"watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors"* (8:34). At the end love and hate are turned over: to hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.

Folly draws by what is hidden. "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", and she calls, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" and "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. The sweetness is what she claims for stolen water. The one who turns in knows the claim and not the end.

section: The heart is hidden, and God sees it
paragraph: The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*. "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death").

Zephaniah calls people to seek before the day comes: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land, who do his just commands; seek righteousness; seek humility; perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zephaniah 2:3). Those called are already humble and already doing his commands, and they are told to seek humility. The verse promises nothing beyond "perhaps", and the hiding is God's to give. What a person has leaned on is tested on that day: "Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death" (Proverbs 11:4).

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
- "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
- "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
- Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21)

section: Life and death set before a person
paragraph:
Death is set before the inner being in the same words: *"Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death"* (Jeremiah 21:8).
- **A way can seem right and still end there.** *"There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death"* (Proverbs 14:12).
- **A choice can be made with death in view.** Esau: *"I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"* (Genesis 25:32).
- **A death can set the direction of a life.** *"he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised"* (2 Corinthians 5:15).
- **A choice between two goods can stay open.** *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).

Proverbs joins life with the fear of the Lord.
- "The fear of the Lord prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short" (Proverbs 10:27).
- "The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death" (Proverbs 14:27).
- "The fear of the Lord leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm" (Proverbs 19:23).

The fear of a threat makes a person run. This fear, in God's own words, keeps a person from turning away. And what it brings is the reverse of what terror brings.
- confidence: "In the fear of the Lord one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge" (Proverbs 14:26)
- life: "a fountain of life" (14:27)
- understanding: "the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7)
- a turning from evil: "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil" (Proverbs 8:13)

The verses join it to:
- turning from evil: "by the fear of the Lord one turns away from evil" (Proverbs 16:6); "The fear of the Lord is hatred of evil" (Proverbs 8:13)
- knowledge: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7)
- confidence: "In the fear of the Lord one has strong confidence" (Proverbs 14:26)
- life: "a fountain of life" (Proverbs 14:27)

Fear touches many of the activities in this Part. The verses join it to the others in their own wording: by paired commands, by "but", by "for" and "so that", and by sharing a root.
- **The heart** (Chapter 4): fear is felt there, given there, and kept out of it: "His heart is steady; he will not be afraid" (Psalm 112:8).
- **Losing heart and courage:** "Do not fear or be dismayed" (Deuteronomy 31:8); "Be strong and courageous. Do not fear" (Deuteronomy 31:6).
- **Knowing and hearing** (10.2): the fear of the Lord is "the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7). It is learned by hearing, and it spreads to "all who heard of it" (Acts 5:5).
- **Speaking** (10.5): fear silences, bends speech, and is told to "go on speaking" (Acts 18:9).
- **Choosing** (10.7): fear holds back the hand.
- **Relating to God** (10.9): the fear of God; "Fear not"; trust.
- **Relating to others** (10.10): fear of man; fear for another; respect owed.
- **Hiding and disclosing** (10.11): fear hides, and fear also comes forward and tells "the whole truth" (Mark 5:33).
- **Feeling** (10.1): fear sits beside anger and grief. One root is shared with both (*rāgaz*).
- **Love, joy and peace:** commanded with love (Deuteronomy 10:12) and cast out by it (1 John 4:18); joined with joy (Psalm 2:11); "none shall make you afraid" with peace (Leviticus 26:6).
- **Going wrong** (Chapter 12): fear that leads to lying and hypocrisy; no fear of God.
- **Under God's anger** (Chapter 13): dread laid on, a horror made, terror as event.
- **Made new** (Chapter 14): fear given in the heart; the spirit not of fear.
- **Life and death** (Chapter 2): the fear of death; the fear of the Lord as "a fountain of life" (Proverbs 14:27).

The death of those who belong to God is seen by him. "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Psalm 116:15). Balaam says, "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). "The righteous finds refuge in his death" (Proverbs 14:32). Hebrews says of the patriarchs, "These all died in faith, not having received the things promised" (Hebrews 11:13), and of Abel, "through his faith, though he died, he still speaks" (Hebrews 11:4). Jesus speaks of a death that bears fruit: "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24).

Each party that comes into anger's verses does so in its own way.
- **The Spirit of God** comes with anger. "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). The Spirit rushed upon Samson, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men; after it, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). Ezekiel, lifted by the Spirit, went "in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me" (Ezekiel 3:14). The anger list in Ephesians is set beside the Spirit grieved (Ephesians 4:30–31).
- **The prophet is filled with God's wrath:** "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (Jeremiah 6:11). "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (Jeremiah 15:17).
- **Angels.** The angel of the Lord stood in Balaam's way, seen by the donkey and not by the man: "God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord took his stand in the way as his adversary" (Numbers 22:22). Balaam's own anger fell on the donkey (22:27). God "let loose on them his burning anger … a company of destroying angels" (Psalm 78:49). An angel asked how long: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem … against which you have been angry these seventy years?", and "the Lord answered gracious and comforting words" (Zechariah 1:12–13).
- **The devil:** "Woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!" (Revelation 12:12).
- **The master in Jesus' parables,** a figure standing for God. "In anger his master delivered him to the jailers" (Matthew 18:34), after "should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (18:33). The applied lesson places the requirement in the hearer's heart: "So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart" (18:35). In another parable the anger turns into a wider invitation: "the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly … and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame'" (Luke 14:21).
- **Onlookers:** "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls … lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (Proverbs 24:17–18).
- **The physical world** bears it. "My anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground" (Jeremiah 7:20). "The foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry" (Psalm 18:7).
- **Enemies' anger,** as the one attacked bears it: "then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us" (Psalm 124:3). Answered by God's hand: "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (Psalm 138:7). And by "do not fear": "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (Isaiah 7:4). "By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king" (Hebrews 11:27).
- **A ruler's anger,** as those beneath it bear it: "A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it" (Proverbs 16:14). "The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life" (20:2). The next verse says what to do instead: "It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling" (20:3).
- **Those who pursue another.** Job's friends say, "How we will pursue him!" and "The root of the matter is found in him" (Job 19:28). He answers them: "be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment" (19:29). He says it straight after "I know that my Redeemer lives" (19:25). I read the one accused as turning the fear of wrath back on those who pursue him, from the confidence he has just spoken.
- **The nations.** In worship the elders say, "The nations raged, but your wrath came" (Revelation 11:18). Two angers stand in one sentence, and the second answers the first. The same verse names the reward of "those who fear your name, both small and great" (10.12; 13.1).

Anger touches many of the activities in this Part. The verses join it to the others in their own wording: by "so", "therefore" and "lest", by "but", by naming them together, and by sharing a root.
- **Fear** (10.12): Moses afraid of the anger, and heard (Deuteronomy 9:19); afraid, then enraged (Daniel 11:30); angry, then afraid (2 Samuel 6:8–9); not afraid of the king's anger (Hebrews 11:27). The two share a root in *rāgaz*, "to tremble", rendered "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4). "Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?" (Psalm 90:11).
- **Feeling** (10.1): anger beside grief. Jonathan "was grieved for David" (1 Samuel 20:34). Jesus was angry and grieved at once (Mark 3:5). "Godly grief produces a repentance", and with it indignation (2 Corinthians 7:10–11).
- **Knowing and hearing** (10.2): anger is kindled on hearing, and God's anger is said to end in knowing (Ezekiel 5:13) and to be understood later (Jeremiah 23:20).
- **Remembering** (10.3): "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath" (Deuteronomy 9:7). When the king's anger abated, "he remembered Vashti" (Esther 2:1).
- **Speaking** (10.5): "A soft answer turns away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1); rash words from an embittered spirit (Psalm 106:33); "slow to speak, slow to anger" (James 1:19).
- **Wanting** (10.6): jealousy with anger (Proverbs 6:34); "You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (James 4:2).
- **Relating to God** (10.9): God's anger, provoked, pleaded against, borne and turned.
- **Relating to others** (10.10): the ruler's anger; strife between people; turning another's anger away.
- **Going wrong** (Chapter 12): the lists of what is put away; "one given to anger causes much transgression" (Proverbs 29:22).
- **Made new** (Chapter 14): putting off anger with the old self (Colossians 3:8–10); delivered from the wrath to come.
- **Life and death** (Chapter 2): "the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36); "A king's wrath is a messenger of death" (Proverbs 16:14).
- **The heart and the spirit** (Chapters 4 and 6): anger burns within, lodges in the heart of fools, and comes in the heat of the spirit.

Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
- "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
- "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
- Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21)

section: From the heart to the mouth
paragraph: Proverbs puts it in one line: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21). The first word spoken against God's command was about death: "But the serpent said to the woman, 'You will not surely die.'" (Genesis 3:4). Chapter 2 ("Death and sin") follows it.

Some of what kills a person is named from within. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Sections 10.1, 10.5 and 10.6 follow these.

Wanting can end in death. James gives the order: "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Wanting is also measured against death. Of the arrogant man, "His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Habakkuk 2:5). And "love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6).

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

A person can have a part in it too:
- "Rescue those who are being taken away to death" (Proverbs 24:11)
- "whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death" (James 5:20)

Some of the last words Scripture records before a death are a blessing or a request:
- Isaac: "that my soul may bless you before I die" (Genesis 27:4)
- Jacob, on seeing Joseph again: "Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive" (Genesis 46:30)
- Joseph: "I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land" (Genesis 50:24)
- "Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die" (Proverbs 30:7)
- "By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff" (Hebrews 11:21)

Joab sent a wise woman of Tekoa to David with a staged plea: "Joab put the words in her mouth" (2 Samuel 14:3). In it she says: "We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). Death falls alike on those the world would set apart:
- "How the wise dies just like the fool!" (Ecclesiastes 2:16)
- "a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2)
- "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27)

section: Breath lent, and held by God
paragraph: In this, humans and animals share one lot: "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). The flood fell on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17), and "Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died" (7:22).

section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
paragraph: **"Animals have souls but not spirits."** The animals are "living creatures", the same phrase as the man in Genesis 2:7. But they also have "the breath of life". The flood came on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17; 7:15), and there the word is *rûaḥ*. "They all have the same breath" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). There is "the spirit of the beast" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). "When you take away their breath, they die" (Psalm 104:29). What marks the man in Genesis 2:7 is not that he has breath and they do not. It is that **God himself breathed it into him**.

paragraph:
Scripture is honest that people sometimes want to die. In the words of Elijah, Jonah, Job and Saul below, the Hebrew word behind "my life" or "I" is *nephesh* ("soul, life"). Most other such wishes name no inner word at all.
- Elijah "asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life'" (1 Kings 19:4).
- Jonah: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).
- Job: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever" (Job 7:15–16). A few verses earlier he spoke of "the anguish of my spirit" and "the bitterness of my soul" (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: "When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions" (7:13–14). He says it to God, "Leave me alone" (7:16), and he does not act on it.
- Saul, wounded on Gilboa: "anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers" (2 Samuel 1:9).
- Job speaks of those "who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures" (Job 3:21), and asks, "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" (Job 3:11).
- Rachel, envying her sister: "Give me children, or I shall die!" (Genesis 30:1).
- The Preacher: "I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

section: Aimed at nothing, and enjoyment given
paragraph:
Yet the same book, four times, commends enjoyment, and each time straight after something he cannot resolve:
- after "he has put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done": "there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live; also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in all his toil — this is God's gift to man" (Ecclesiastes 3:11–13)
- after the rich man whose "full stomach … will not let him sleep" and who "all his days … eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:12, 17): "what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil … the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot" (5:18)
- after the righteous who are treated as the wicked: "And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful" (8:14–15)
- and at the start: "There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?" (2:24–25). "For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy" (2:26).

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

Desire can take hold in the heart before anything is done. Jesus says, "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). The way in is the eye, and he goes straight on: "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away" (5:29). Proverbs warns a son in the same order, heart and eyes: "Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes" (Proverbs 6:25). The Preacher uses the hunter's picture for the other side of that capture: "the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her" (Ecclesiastes 7:26). He names it as his own finding, after he had "turned my heart to know and to search out" (7:25). The escape he names is not strength of will but pleasing God.

section: Breath lent, and held by God
paragraph:
Life is held in the breath, and the breath is God's to give and to take back.
- "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).
- Daniel tells a king who had praised idols that he had not honoured "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways" (Daniel 5:23).
- "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (Job 34:14–15).
- "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30).
- "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
- "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psalm 146:4). Thinking goes when the breath goes. "Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow" (Psalm 144:4), and the Lord "knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).

paragraph: **Ruling within.** Even the verses in which a person rules inside himself join the rule to another act. "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). "Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). A man "having his desire under control" (1 Corinthians 7:37). "'All things are lawful for me,' but I will not be dominated by anything" (1 Corinthians 6:12): what a man is free to do can come to rule him. Elsewhere God is asked: "Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me!" (Psalm 19:13). Or it is grace: "sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace" (Romans 6:14), with the command two verses before, "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body" (6:12). And one thing no one rules: "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).

paragraph: The living are weighed too. "But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion" (Ecclesiastes 9:4). The verse before it says what is in the living: "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live" (9:3). And before God, "no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Chapter 12 follows this.

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph: Scripture speaks of the heart while a person lives: "madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). I have found no verse that speaks of the heart after death.

The Preacher says the heart's state lasts as long as the life: "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). The psalmist asks not to be judged, "for no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Paul traces a life cut off from God to the heart: "alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Life weighed", "Death in the living") gives the setting.

The living are weighed too. "But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion" (Ecclesiastes 9:4). The verse before it says what is in the living: "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live" (9:3). And before God, "no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Chapter 12 follows this.

Scripture also speaks of the dead from this side of death, and there it says something different. The dead are silent and gone:
- "But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?" (Job 14:10)
- "For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
- "For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?" (Psalm 6:5)
- "The dead do not praise the Lord, nor do any who go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17)
- Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (Psalm 49:19)

Wanting can end in death. James gives the order: "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Wanting is also measured against death. Of the arrogant man, "His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Habakkuk 2:5). And "love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6).

In the Song, love has its own time. Three times the bride charges the daughters of Jerusalem, "that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7; 3:5; 8:4). Each time it follows love already felt: love-sickness (2:5), finding and holding (3:4), longing (8:1–2). It is said to others, and "until it pleases" is the delight word. Love is not to be roused early, or roused by anyone else. The one awakening in the book is the beloved's: "Under the apple tree I awakened you" (8:5). And straight after it, what love is once roused: "love is strong as death … Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised" (8:6–7). It cannot be roused before its time, and once roused it cannot be put out and cannot be bought.

- **The throat or neck.** "Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck [*nephesh*]" (Psalm 69:1). "His neck was put in a collar of iron" (Psalm 105:18).
- **Appetite.** "Put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite" (Proverbs 23:2). Throat and appetite stand side by side. "A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on" (Proverbs 16:26). Even Sheol, the grave, "has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth" (Isaiah 5:14).
- **Desire and longing.** "As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God" (Psalm 42:1).
- **Life.** People "seek my life", "save his life", give "life for life". Naomi's grandson will be "a restorer of life" (Ruth 4:15). A millstone may not be taken in pledge, "for that would be taking a life in pledge" (Deuteronomy 24:6). Livelihood is life.
- **Myself.** On the Day of Atonement, "you shall afflict yourselves" (Leviticus 16:29), literally your souls. "As you yourself live" (2 Kings 2:2).
- **A person.** "Seventy persons" went down to Egypt (Exodus 1:5). "Three thousand souls" were added at Pentecost (Acts 2:41).
- **A living creature.** Fish, birds and beasts are "living creatures" (Genesis 1:20–24), and so is the man (Genesis 2:7).
- **A dead body.** "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11). The word is *nephesh*.

- **Prayer lives in the heart.** It can be complete there without a voice (1 Samuel 1:13). "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lamentations 2:19). "With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O Lord!" (Psalm 119:145).
- **God speaks to the heart.** To comfort someone, in Hebrew, is to *speak to their heart*. Joseph "comforted them and spoke kindly to them" (Genesis 50:21), literally to their hearts. God says of his people, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her" (Hosea 2:14), again to her heart. "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:2).
- **Comforted as by a mother.** "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 66:13). Before it the people are pictured as infants: "that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance" (66:11), "carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees" (66:12). The act is being comforted. The delight is the infant's, in being fed, and the one who comforts is God (13.1).
- **God tests the heart.** "The Lord tests hearts" (Proverbs 17:3). And he forgives according to what he knows there: "render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39).
- **The soul is the self in address.** It is told to bless, to hope and to rest (Chapter 5).
- **Life is asked of him.** "Give me life" runs through Psalm 119, and each time it rests on something in God: "give me life according to your word!" (Psalm 119:25); "In your steadfast love give me life" (119:88). The life asked for is for keeping his word, praising him and calling on him: "Let my soul live and praise you" (119:175); "give us life, and we will call upon your name!" (Psalm 80:18). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **He holds the breath.** Daniel to a king who had praised idols: "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored" (Daniel 5:23).
- **Seeing and hearing him, and living.** "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Israel marvelled: "This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live" (Deuteronomy 5:24). Manoah feared the same: "We shall surely die, for we have seen God" (Judges 13:22). To Gideon God said, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die" (Judges 6:23).
- **Relied on in the face of death.** "we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Chapter 2 ("Facing death") gives the account.
- **Asked for a brother.** "If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life" (1 John 5:16).
- **Inquired of, not the dead.** "should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?" (Isaiah 8:19).
- **Told to depart.** Those who "spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol" (Job 21:13) "say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'" (21:14–15). The act is a sending away. It is argued as a sum: serving and praying are weighed for profit and found not worth it. Job answers, "The counsel of the wicked is far from me" (21:16).
- **Returned to.** Eliphaz counsels Job: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up" (Job 22:21–23). Then "the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver" (22:25), and "you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you" (22:26–27). The act is returning. Delight comes after it, and prayer after the delight. It is a friend's counsel, given as a condition.
- **The human spirit worships.** "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24). "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47). Paul serves God "with my spirit" (Romans 1:9). At death the spirit is what is committed into God's hands.
- **God's Spirit prays within.** "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). The Spirit "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit" (Romans 8:26–27). The cry to God rises from inside the heart, and it is God's own Spirit crying.
- **God knows the leaning before the deed.** "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- **God reveals in the night.** "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries … Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these" (Daniel 2:28).
- **God reckons, and faith reckons.** God counted Abraham's faith "to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). "Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Romans 4:8). Abraham, for his part, "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19).
- **His plans against are open to turning.** "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds" (Jeremiah 26:3). How his own plans work is in 13.1 (*Purposing*).
- **Plotting is turned against him.** "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hosea 7:15). The verse before shows the same people: "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (7:14). Nahum asks, "What do you plot against the Lord?" (Nahum 1:9), and names "one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (1:11). Plotting against people is in 10.10.
- **His word can be reckoned strange, and his name esteemed.** "Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hosea 8:12). Against that stand "those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name" (Malachi 3:16), whom "the Lord paid attention and heard".
- **Thinking done in his presence sees differently.** "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). What he had been thinking about was envy: "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3). In the sanctuary he sees it as "a dream when one awakes" (73:20; 10.6, *Jealousy and envy*).
- **God cannot be likened.** "To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?" (Isaiah 40:18). And God rebukes those who thought him "one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21).
- **The heart meditates on him.** "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **And he thinks of me.** "What is man that you regard him, or the son of man that you think of him?" (Psalm 144:3). "I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). And his thoughts are precious to the one he knows: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).
- **Sought, and not far.** Paul tells the Athenians that God set the times and places of the nations *"that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us"* (Acts 17:27). The seeking is a groping in the dark; the one sought is close by. The next verse is *"In him we live and move and have our being"* (17:28; Chapter 2).
- **Recognised, and gone to.** At the lake, *"That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!' When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land"* (John 21:7–8). One sees and says it; one hears and leaps; the others come in with the catch. I read the same recognition met in three ways, none of them rebuked.

section: Pride and the lifted-up heart and spirit
paragraph: Death brings pride down. In Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), the dead greet him: "You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us! Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers" (14:10–11).

"We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:51–53). Then Isaiah's word comes to pass: "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54; Isaiah 25:8). "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55). Hosea had already said it: "I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" (Hosea 13:14).

And the dead will wake. "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). The waking is not the same for all. Isaiah sets two kinds of dead side by side: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (Isaiah 26:14), and "You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!" (26:19). For the psalmist, waking means seeing God: "when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15). These verses are followed below, in "The body raised" and "Life, and judgment". Job's "he will not awake" stands beside them, and I do not reconcile the two.

The hope Scripture gives does not leave the body behind. Job says it of his own flesh: "For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth. And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!" (Job 19:25–27). The psalmist says it of waking: "As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15).
- "Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! … the earth will give birth to the dead" (Isaiah 26:19).
- A few verses earlier, of other lords: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (26:14).
- "After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him" (Hosea 6:2).
