- "After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him" (Hosea 6:2).

What is precious can be a refuge. God lays *"a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste'"* (Isaiah 28:16). He says it to scoffers who had made another refuge: *"we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter"* (28:15). The one who believes is not hurried. Peter takes up the stone, *"a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6), and adds, *"So the honor is for you who believe"* (2:7).
There is a false shelter too: "we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15).

The fear of dying shapes what people do. Isaac passed off his wife as his sister: "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'" (Genesis 26:9). God asks his people, "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass" (Isaiah 51:12). Hebrews names that fear as bondage: Christ shared flesh and blood "that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery" (Hebrews 2:14–15). Section 10.1 follows fear.

Forgetting God also makes room for fear. "Who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker … and you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor" (Isaiah 51:12–13). Fear of someone's anger grows where God is forgotten.

Fear of man is answered the same way, by turning to God. "Who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The fear of man goes with forgetting God, and it is answered by remembering who made you. Isaiah is told to turn his fear and his dread onto the Lord himself (Isaiah 8:12–13; 10.1).

Fear of other people takes several forms in the verses.
- **Fear of man.** "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies" (Isaiah 51:12). "do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28).
- **Fear for another.** Eli trembled for the ark (1 Samuel 4:13). Jeremiah grieved for his people: "For the wound of the daughter of my people is my heart wounded; I mourn, and dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21). Paul: "I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3).
- **Fear used as a tool.** "he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin" (Nehemiah 6:13).
- **Respect owed.** The same word as fear is rendered "respect" toward people. "respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed" (Romans 13:7). "Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1 Peter 2:18). Toward parents: "Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father" (Leviticus 19:3).
- **Respect and no fear, two verses apart.** "Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:14–15). In Greek, "fear" and "respect" are the same word. The verse does not say whether the respect is toward the one who asks or toward God.
- **Being feared.** Being feared works on the one who is feared. "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16).

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

The making alive rests on a death:
- "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3)
- "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8)
- "so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone" (Hebrews 2:9)
- God himself calls for it: "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me … Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (Zechariah 13:7). Jesus reads it of his own death on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:31).
- Isaiah says it of the soul: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12)

The living can also feel themselves among the dead. "like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more" (Psalm 88:5). "For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground; he has made me sit in darkness like those long dead" (Psalm 143:3). "among those in full vigor we are like dead men" (Isaiah 59:10). It is on "those dwelling in the region and shadow of death" that "a light has dawned" (Matthew 4:16).

Under judgment, death is chosen over life: "Death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family" (Jeremiah 8:3). "Preferred" is the choosing word. It is said as part of a judgment the Lord declares. Before it, the bones of the dead are spread "before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they have loved and served, which they have gone after" (8:2). The verse does not say that the one leads to the other. In Revelation death is sought and not found: "people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them" (Revelation 9:6). And Job's wife urges it on him: "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die" (Job 2:9).

section: Pleading, and standing in the breach
paragraph:
But the breach is not always filled.
- "I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none" (Ezekiel 22:30).
- Even the best could only save themselves: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (Ezekiel 14:20).
- Jeremiah, who had stood before God "to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them", found that "they have dug a pit for my life". He then prayed for the anger to fall on them (Jeremiah 18:20–23).

section: Pleading, and standing in the breach
paragraph:
But the breach is not always filled.
- "I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none" (Ezekiel 22:30).
- Even the best could only save themselves: "even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it … they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness" (Ezekiel 14:20).
- Jeremiah, who had stood before God "to speak good for them, to turn away your wrath from them", found that "they have dug a pit for my life". He then prayed for the anger to fall on them (Jeremiah 18:20–23).

Death is set before a person just as plainly. "See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil" (Deuteronomy 30:15). "Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Proverbs marks where the other way ends:
- "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12)
- "In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death" (Proverbs 12:28)
- Wisdom: "For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the Lord, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:35–36). To hate wisdom is to love death, a love the person does not know he has.
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits" (Proverbs 18:21)

section: Life and death set before a person
paragraph:
Death is set before the inner being in the same words: *"Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death"* (Jeremiah 21:8).
- **A way can seem right and still end there.** *"There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death"* (Proverbs 14:12).
- **A choice can be made with death in view.** Esau: *"I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"* (Genesis 25:32).
- **A death can set the direction of a life.** *"he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised"* (2 Corinthians 5:15).
- **A choice between two goods can stay open.** *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).

Grief at a death takes more than one form:
- David fasted while his child lived, and rose when he died: "But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?" (2 Samuel 12:23).
- Later, "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead" (2 Samuel 13:39).
- Jeremiah turns the weeping elsewhere: "Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away" (Jeremiah 22:10).
- Mary, at Jesus' feet: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (John 11:32).

Fear does not stay inside. It moves the person, and the verses follow where it moves them.
- **It drives away.** Adam hid. Uriah "was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt" (Jeremiah 26:21). At Sinai "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off" (Exodus 20:18).
- **It holds back the hand.** "The young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid" (Judges 8:20). Section 10.7 follows this.
- **It silences.** "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). Section 10.5 follows this.
- **It bends speech into a lie.** Sarah said "I did not laugh," "for she was afraid" (Genesis 18:15).
- **It takes the wrong voice.** "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). Section 10.8 follows this.
- **It hardens.** It began because "the Lord was with him but had departed from Saul" (1 Samuel 18:12). It ended: "Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually" (18:29).
- **It spreads.** The fearful man is sent home "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8).
- **It stays, and what it fears can follow.** "The sword that you fear shall overtake you there" (Jeremiah 42:16). "For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me" (Job 3:25). Under the curse it fills every hour: "In the morning you shall say, 'If only it were evening!' and at evening you shall say, 'If only it were morning!'" (Deuteronomy 28:67).

**Fear can set a direction as well as stop one.**
- Uriah *"was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt"* (Jeremiah 26:21).
- The rulers of Samaria, told by Jehu to set up a king and fight, "were exceedingly afraid and said, 'Behold, the two kings could not stand before him. How then can we stand?'" (2 Kings 10:4). They gave up the choice: "We are your servants, and we will do all that you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do whatever is good in your eyes" (10:5). The next letter used what they had handed over: "take the heads of your master's sons" (10:6).
- When the hail was announced, *"whoever feared the word of the Lord among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses, but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the Lord left his slaves and his livestock in the field"* (Exodus 9:20–21). The fear of God's word is what made the difference in what people did.
- Proverbs turns the same word into a quality of the wise: *"One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless"* (Proverbs 14:16). "Cautious" renders the fear word.

The verses follow fear into what the person does next. Some of these lead away from God and from others, and some lead toward them.
- **It hides and keeps away.** "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). At Sinai "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off" (Exodus 20:18). Joseph of Arimathea was a disciple "secretly for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38). The disciples met "the doors being locked … for fear of the Jews" (John 20:19). Section 10.11 follows this.
- **It flees.** Uriah "was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt" (Jeremiah 26:21).
- **It silences.** "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). "Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him" (John 7:13). "They did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him" (Mark 9:32). Section 10.5 follows this.
- **It bends speech and conduct.** Sarah said she did not laugh, "for she was afraid" (Genesis 18:15). Saul: "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). At Antioch Peter "drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party. And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him" (Galatians 2:12–13).
- **It holds back the hand, but not the wish.** "The young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid" (Judges 8:20). The chief priests were "seeking to arrest him", but "they feared the crowds" (Matthew 21:46). Herod "wanted to put him to death", but "he feared the people" (Matthew 14:5). The arrest is not made. The verses do not say the wish has changed.
- **It stops the will.** Saul's armor-bearer "would not, for he feared greatly" (1 Samuel 31:4). "David was afraid of the Lord that day … So David was not willing to take the ark" (2 Samuel 6:9–10). Israel "would not go up" when "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (Deuteronomy 1:26, 28). In David's case what he heard next moved him again (2 Samuel 6:12). 10.7 (*Willing*) follows the will.
- **It hardens into enmity.** "Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually" (1 Samuel 18:29).
- **It spreads.** The fearful man is sent home "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8). "Great fear came upon all who heard of it" (Acts 5:5).
- **It turns to God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). "Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 20:3). Peter, sinking: "Lord, save me" (Matthew 14:30).
- **It comes forward and tells the truth.** The woman healed of her bleeding, "knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth" (Mark 5:33). The jailer, "trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas", asked, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" (Acts 16:29–30).
- **It glorifies God, or asks him to go.** "When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God" (Matthew 9:8). But when the Gerasenes saw the healed man, they "asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear" (Luke 8:37). Felix, hearing of "righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment", "was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present'" (Acts 24:25).
- **It asks a question.** "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). "What then will this child be?" (Luke 1:66).

It is tempting to turn this verse into a formula: body plus breath equals soul. I have stopped doing that. It is not an equation of parts. Scripture speaks of God making every side of the person:
- "the Lord … who made our souls" (Jeremiah 38:16)
- God "formed the spirit of man within him" (Zechariah 12:1)
- "The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life" (Job 33:4)

paragraph:
Fear does not stay inside. It moves the person, and the verses follow where it moves them.
- **It drives away.** Adam hid. Uriah "was afraid and fled and escaped to Egypt" (Jeremiah 26:21). At Sinai "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off" (Exodus 20:18).
- **It holds back the hand.** "The young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid" (Judges 8:20). Section 10.7 follows this.
- **It silences.** "Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). Section 10.5 follows this.
- **It bends speech into a lie.** Sarah said "I did not laugh," "for she was afraid" (Genesis 18:15).
- **It takes the wrong voice.** "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). Section 10.8 follows this.
- **It hardens.** It began because "the Lord was with him but had departed from Saul" (1 Samuel 18:12). It ended: "Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually" (18:29).
- **It spreads.** The fearful man is sent home "lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8).
- **It stays, and what it fears can follow.** "The sword that you fear shall overtake you there" (Jeremiah 42:16). "For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me" (Job 3:25). Under the curse it fills every hour: "In the morning you shall say, 'If only it were evening!' and at evening you shall say, 'If only it were morning!'" (Deuteronomy 28:67).

In the verses, anxiety gains nothing for the thing it is about, and it does several things to the person.
- **It adds nothing.** "Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" (Matthew 6:27).
- **It runs ahead.** "Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble" (6:34).
- **It weighs the heart down.** "Watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap" (Luke 21:34).
- **It chokes what has been received.** In the parable of the sower, "the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful" (Matthew 13:22). Against it Luke sets those who "hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience" (Luke 8:15).
- **Many things against one.** Martha "was distracted with much serving" (Luke 10:40). Jesus says: "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (10:41–42). Paul says the married man is anxious about pleasing his wife, "and his interests are divided" (1 Corinthians 7:34). What Paul wants is "undivided devotion to the Lord" (7:35).
- **What it fears can follow.** "The famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you to Egypt" (Jeremiah 42:16). The people had gone to Egypt to get away from it.

Some wanting is fear underneath. After Jerusalem fell, the remnant asked Jeremiah for God's word: "whatever the Lord our God says, declare to us and we will do it" (Jeremiah 42:20). God answered with a promise: "Do not fear the king of Babylon … for I am with you" (42:11). They wanted the opposite: "No, we will go to the land of Egypt, where we shall not see war or hear the sound of the trumpet or be hungry for bread" (42:14). The place is wanted for what is absent there: no war, no trumpet, no hunger. The verses name what lies underneath: "the sword that you fear shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close after you" (42:16). And so "you shall die … in the place where you desire to go to live" (42:22). I read that what they wanted was not Egypt but to be free of what they feared, and that the fear went with them.

section: Fear that comes upon a person
paragraph: And it can stay, or come again. "For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me" (Job 3:25). "The sword that you fear shall overtake you there" (Jeremiah 42:16). Afterwards it is turned over in the mind: "Your heart will muse on the terror" (Isaiah 33:18).

The sleep can be laid on as judgment. Of Babylon the Lord says, "While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake" (Jeremiah 51:39). The merriment itself leads into the sleep.

A person can be answerable for another's death, or turn another back from it. God tells Ezekiel, "If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning … that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand" (Ezekiel 3:18). "Whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death" (James 5:20). John makes love the sign of life itself: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). And kindness reaches even the dead: "May he be blessed by the Lord, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" (Ruth 2:20).

Life can also be wrongly kept or taken by words. God condemns those who were "putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies" (Ezekiel 13:19).

section: The soul is hunted and rescued
paragraph: Because the soul is the life, it is the thing at stake. Enemies "seek my life". The false prophetesses hunt souls like birds (Ezekiel 13:18–20). And the soul is what God delivers: "You have delivered my soul from death" (Psalm 116:8). "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). Words reach it too: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25).

section: From the heart to the mouth
paragraph: False words can reach life itself. God condemns the prophetesses "putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies" (Ezekiel 13:19). "You have disheartened the righteous falsely, although I have not grieved him" (13:22).

Each person answers for his own. "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). "But each one shall die for his own sin" (2 Kings 14:6). Jesus says it of unbelief: "unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins" (John 8:24). John speaks of "sin that leads to death" and of sin that does not, and tells a believer to ask life for a brother whose sin does not lead to death (1 John 5:16–17). He does not say which sin leads to death, and I do not guess.

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
paragraph: **"The soul sins; the human spirit never does."** It is true that "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but there the soul means the *person*, the one who answers for the sin. And while I find no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin", the spirit is plainly judged. It is "haughty" before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). It was "not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). It is hardened (Deuteronomy 2:30). It needs to be made "right" (Psalm 51:10). It has or lacks "deceit" (Psalm 32:2). It needs cleansing from "defilement" (2 Corinthians 7:1). If Scripture has a *moral centre*, it is the heart (Chapter 12). The spirit stands beside it, not above it.

The soul can also be harmed by its own wrongdoing: "he who fails to find me injures himself" (Proverbs 8:36).

paragraph: God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" The answer comes at once: "turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:10–11).

**What he has no pleasure in.** *"Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?"* (Ezekiel 18:23). It is said to people who accuse him: *"Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just'"* (18:25). He ends, *"make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live"* (18:31–32). He says it again to people in despair, who ask, *"Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?"* (33:10). This time it is on oath: *"As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live"* (33:11). The same words answer accusing and despairing. I read that his pleasure is told to the inner state of the hearer.

God remembers too, and his remembering changes things.
- He remembers what we are: "he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:39). In that psalm this is his reason for holding back his anger.
- He is asked to remember mercy inside his anger: "in wrath remember mercy" (Habakkuk 3:2).
- He is asked not to remember sin: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (Psalm 79:8).
- He stops remembering when a person turns, either way. Of the wicked who turns: "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezekiel 18:22). Of the righteous who turns to injustice: "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
- Job asks to be hidden "until your wrath be past" and then "remember me!" (Job 14:13).
- He keeps a book of remembrance of those who feared him (Malachi 3:16).
- And he remembers in judgment: "God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath" (Revelation 16:19).

The turning is a considered act, and it reaches back over the past:
- "Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die" (Ezekiel 18:28).
- "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (18:22).
- It reaches back the other way too: when a righteous man turns to injustice, "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).

section: Life and death set before a person
paragraph: Scripture sets life itself before the inner being as a choice. *"I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live"* (Deuteronomy 30:19). The passage says what choosing life is: *"loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days"* (30:20). It describes the other way from inside: *"if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them"* (30:17). Before the choice is set out, it says the choice can be made: *"the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it"* (30:14). Turning that chooses life is a considered act: *"Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die"* (Ezekiel 18:28). Chapter 2 gives the account.

The turning is a considered act, and it reaches back over the past:
- "Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die" (Ezekiel 18:28).
- "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (18:22).
- It reaches back the other way too: when a righteous man turns to injustice, "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).

section: The heart is hidden, and God sees it
paragraph: The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*. "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death").

paragraph: God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" The answer comes at once: "turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:10–11).

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

The prophet's own delight was taken first, and he was told not to mourn it.

*Held (working note, not part of the text):* the verses in which fear crosses into life and death are kept for Chapter 2, where that placement is on hold. Fear of death (Hebrews 2:15) and "the cowardly" (Revelation 21:8) are named above only as fear.

God says what he wants. "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord God, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?" (Ezekiel 18:23). "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (18:32). He says it to people who had given up: "Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?" God swears by his own life, and the oath carries both what he wants and what he will do. "As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). "As I live, declares the Lord God, I will not be inquired of by you" (Ezekiel 20:3). Paul quotes it of the end: "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God" (Romans 14:11).

It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:51–53). Then Isaiah's word comes to pass: "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54; Isaiah 25:8). "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55). Hosea had already said it: "I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" (Hosea 13:14).

Scripture is honest that people sometimes want to die. In the words of Elijah, Jonah, Job and Saul below, the Hebrew word behind "my life" or "I" is *nephesh* ("soul, life"). Most other such wishes name no inner word at all.
- Elijah "asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life'" (1 Kings 19:4).
- Jonah: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:3).
- Job: "I would choose strangling and death rather than my bones. I loathe my life; I would not live forever" (Job 7:15–16). A few verses earlier he spoke of "the anguish of my spirit" and "the bitterness of my soul" (7:11). The wish comes out of his nights: "When I say, 'My bed will comfort me' … then you scare me with dreams and terrify me with visions" (7:13–14). He says it to God, "Leave me alone" (7:16), and he does not act on it.
- Saul, wounded on Gilboa: "anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers" (2 Samuel 1:9).
- Job speaks of those "who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures" (Job 3:21), and asks, "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?" (Job 3:11).
- Rachel, envying her sister: "Give me children, or I shall die!" (Genesis 30:1).
- The Preacher: "I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive" (Ecclesiastes 4:2).

section: Loving and hating one's own soul
paragraph: There is a third kind of hating one's life, and each verse gives its own ground. Job: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1). The Preacher: "So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). Jonah asked to die because God had spared Nineveh: "for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful … Therefore now, O Lord, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:2–3). God answered with a question about his anger: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4). Only the second time did the wish come with faintness, when "the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint" (4:8). I looked at these death-wishes, and how they are answered, in Chapter 2.

section: Loving and hating one's own soul
paragraph: There is a third kind of hating one's life, and each verse gives its own ground. Job: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1). The Preacher: "So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). Jonah asked to die because God had spared Nineveh: "for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful … Therefore now, O Lord, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (Jonah 4:2–3). God answered with a question about his anger: "Do you do well to be angry?" (4:4). Only the second time did the wish come with faintness, when "the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint" (4:8). I looked at these death-wishes, and how they are answered, in Chapter 2.

What answers these wishes is seldom death.
- **Elijah** is given food, twice: "Arise and eat". He goes "in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights" (1 Kings 19:5–8).
- **Jonah's** wish came with his anger at God's mercy: "angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9). He is given a question about God's pity for Nineveh (Jonah 4:10–11).
- **Israel**, wishing they had died beside the meat pots of Egypt, is given bread from heaven (Exodus 16:3–4).
- When Israel loathed the manna and spoke against God, the answer was something to look at: "everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live" (Numbers 21:8).

A feeling can turn back on the one who has it. "You who tear yourself in your anger" (Job 18:4). Joseph forbids it: "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here" (Genesis 45:5). Jonah, angry at God's mercy, asks to die: "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9).

Wanting can end in death. James gives the order: "Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death" (James 1:15). "The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor" (Proverbs 21:25). Wanting is also measured against death. Of the arrogant man, "His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough" (Habakkuk 2:5). And "love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6).

The living can also feel themselves among the dead. "like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more" (Psalm 88:5). "For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground; he has made me sit in darkness like those long dead" (Psalm 143:3). "among those in full vigor we are like dead men" (Isaiah 59:10). It is on "those dwelling in the region and shadow of death" that "a light has dawned" (Matthew 4:16).

Jesus speaks of death as sleep. "the girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him" (Matthew 9:24). Of Lazarus, "Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep" (John 11:13). Paul uses the same word of those who die believing: "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

Some hold to another even to death:
- Ruth to Naomi: "Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the Lord do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you" (Ruth 1:17).
- Ittai to David: "wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21).
- Peter: "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!" (Matthew 26:35).
- Paul, to friends who wept: "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 21:13).

Scripture does not make the coming of death a calm thing. It shows the inner being under it:
- "My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me" (Psalm 55:4)
- David to Jonathan: "there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3)
- "Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death" (Psalm 13:3)
- In Gethsemane: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38)

section: Soul, spirit and heart at death
paragraph:
**The soul.**
- **It departs.** "As her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni" (Genesis 35:18).
- **It dies.** Balaam: "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" (Numbers 23:10). Samson: "Let me die with the Philistines" (Judges 16:30). In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. And "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4).
- **It is poured out.** Of the servant: "he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). Before his death Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
- **It is named to the very end.** Even the corpse is *nephesh* ("soul"): "Whoever touches the dead body of any person" (Numbers 19:11).
- **It has an end beyond death, and Psalm 49 names two.** The psalm is about the death that comes to everyone: "even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish" (Psalm 49:10). Of the man who trusts in his wealth: "his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light" (49:19). Of himself, the psalmist says: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (49:15). The psalm does not say what being received involves, and I do not fill it in. Of those who trust in their wealth it says, "death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning" (49:14), and it draws a word for the living from this: "Be not afraid when a man becomes rich" (49:16).
- **It is not abandoned.** David wrote, "you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption" (Psalm 16:10). Peter reads it of Christ's death and rising: "he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption" (Acts 2:31).

The soul is where bitterness lives. Hannah was "deeply distressed" (bitter of soul, 1 Samuel 1:10). So were David's men at Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:6), and Job: "I will complain in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 7:11). The soul is "cast down" and "in turmoil" (Psalm 42:5), "bowed down to the dust" (Psalm 44:25), "poured out" (1 Samuel 1:15; Job 30:16). It "refuses to be comforted" (Psalm 77:2). Samson's soul was "vexed to death" (Judges 16:16). Jesus said, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38), and "Now is my soul troubled" (John 12:27).

section: The willing spirit and the weak flesh
paragraph: The most human scene with flesh in it is Gethsemane. Jesus says, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me" (Matthew 26:38). He prays, "not as I will, but as you will" (26:39). He finds the disciples asleep and says, "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). Then he finds them sleeping again, "for their eyes were heavy" (26:43).

What was seen can be covered with money and a story. The guards *"told the chief priests all that had taken place"* (Matthew 28:11). The elders *"gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers and said, 'Tell people, His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep. And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble'"* (28:12–14). *"So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day"* (28:15). The truth was told to them first; they paid to hide it, and promised safety to those who carried the lie.

And with God, the dead are carried, blessed and at rest:
- "The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side" (Luke 16:22)
- "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on." "Blessed indeed," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them!" (Revelation 14:13)
- David, of his dead child: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me" (2 Samuel 12:23)
- Jesus, answering a question about the resurrection: "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38)
- "who died for us so that whether we are awake or asleep we might live with him" (1 Thessalonians 5:10)
- The psalmist: "But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me" (Psalm 49:15)
- To the man dying beside him: "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43)
- Paul, weighing life and death: "My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account" (Philippians 1:23–24)
- "we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In the same chapter he says, "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed" (5:4, in "Waited for", above). Both are stated
- Peter: "the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does" (1 Peter 4:6)

In the resurrection, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven" (Matthew 22:30). Luke gives the reason: "for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" (Luke 20:36). "Death shall be no more" (Revelation 21:4).

In these verses the dead who are made alive are living people, "dead in your trespasses". "God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). Jesus says the crossing happens now: "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life" (John 5:24). "If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death" (John 8:51); "everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?" (John 11:26). The life given is spoken of as had now and as still to come. "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life" (John 6:47); "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). Jesus also promises "in the age to come eternal life" (Mark 10:30). Scripture states both. John gives a sign that the crossing has happened: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). Paul says it is meant to show in the way a person lives: "just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).

- **The lowly spirit and the contrite heart revived:** "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15). God's reason is tender: "I will not contend forever … for the spirit would grow faint before me" (57:16).
- **The soul restored:** "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). "The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul" (Psalm 19:7). "Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (James 1:21). "Having purified your souls by your obedience to the truth" (1 Peter 1:22).
- **The conscience cleansed:** "the blood of Christ … [will] purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). "Let us draw near with a true heart … with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience" (Hebrews 10:22).
- **The mind renewed:** "be renewed in the spirit of your minds" (Ephesians 4:23). "Be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2).
- **The inner self renewed daily:** "Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16).
- **The whole person transformed:** "We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:18).
- **The straying spirit and the murmuring mouth taught:** "those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction" (Isaiah 29:24).
- **The life kept hidden:** "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).
- **Born again to a living hope:** God "has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). Paul: "that I may know him and the power of his resurrection" (Philippians 3:10).
- **The mortal body given life:** "he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). The body itself is still waited for: "we … groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). Chapter 2 ("The body raised") gives the account.
- **The dead in trespasses made alive:** "you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life … has passed from death to life" (John 5:24).
- **Died to sin, and to the law:** "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). "For one who has died has been set free from sin" (Romans 6:7). "For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God" (Galatians 2:19). "we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit" (Romans 7:6).
- **What is earthly put to death:** "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5). "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).
- **Resting on his death:** "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). "he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised" (2 Corinthians 5:15). Chapter 2 ("Made alive") gives the account.
- **Turned, and living:** "For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God; so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32). Chapter 2 gives the account.

Each person answers for his own. "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4). "But each one shall die for his own sin" (2 Kings 14:6). Jesus says it of unbelief: "unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins" (John 8:24). John speaks of "sin that leads to death" and of sin that does not, and tells a believer to ask life for a brother whose sin does not lead to death (1 John 5:16–17). He does not say which sin leads to death, and I do not guess.

In these verses the dead who are made alive are living people, "dead in your trespasses". "God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). Jesus says the crossing happens now: "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life" (John 5:24). "If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death" (John 8:51); "everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?" (John 11:26). The life given is spoken of as had now and as still to come. "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life" (John 6:47); "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). Jesus also promises "in the age to come eternal life" (Mark 10:30). Scripture states both. John gives a sign that the crossing has happened: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). Paul says it is meant to show in the way a person lives: "just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). "For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God" (Colossians 3:3).

Jesus speaks of death as sleep. "the girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him" (Matthew 9:24). Of Lazarus, "Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep" (John 11:13). Paul uses the same word of those who die believing: "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

And Scripture names life itself as a person. Moses says of the Lord, "he is your life and length of days" (Deuteronomy 30:20). Paul speaks of "Christ who is your life" (Colossians 3:4). At Lazarus's grave Jesus says it of himself: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). Jesus says where his own life comes from, and where his people's comes from: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself" (John 5:26); "Because I live, you also will live" (John 14:19). And he says what life is: "this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3).

In these verses the dead who are made alive are living people, "dead in your trespasses". "God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). "Even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). Jesus says the crossing happens now: "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life" (John 5:24). "If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death" (John 8:51); "everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?" (John 11:26). "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life" (John 6:47); "I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13).
